title: Runbook publishing CI/CD retrospective and automation specification
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary
-------
This page captures the retrospective findings from our 2026 program to automate runbook publishing ("Runbook CI/CD"), and publishes a concrete automation specification for how teams should test, lint, release, and monitor runbook changes going forward. The goal: reduce time-to-publish, eliminate stale/incorrect runbooks, and make runbook changes auditable and reversible.

Background
----------
Over 2025–Q1 2026 the eng-platform team piloted a set of automation experiments: runbook linting, preview builds, auto-linking to dashboards, and a gated publish pipeline. The pilot improved throughput but surfaced class-of-failure patterns (broken links, outdated run steps, test flakiness, review bottlenecks). This retrospective summarizes what worked, what didn't, and provides a standardized CI/CD spec for runbooks.

Key metrics we tracked
- Median time from PR opened to published page: 48h -> target 6h.
- Fraction of runbook PRs reverted within 7 days due to errors: 12% -> target <1%.
- CI pass rate for runbook PRs (first run): 78% (goal 95%).
- Broken link detections found by automation vs. operator reports: 7:1

Observations and root causes
1) Linting and validation caught many surface errors but not semantic correctness.
   - Root cause: single-layer checks (YAML/schema/link) do not validate commands or required permissions.
2) Preview builds reduced reviewer friction but reviewers ignored automated preview links when the PR changed multiple times.
   - Root cause: preview URL drift; caching produced stale previews.
3) Ownership and review queues were shared across many teams leading to large review latencies.
   - Root cause: no enforced reviewer on-call rota; no automatic reassignment after 48h.
4) Rollbacks were manual and inconsistent. Some rollbacks introduced more problems.
   - Root cause: lack of atomic publish artifacts and lacking a simple rollback command.

Decisions and design principles (summary)
- Every runbook change must pass automated checks before a human review is required.
- CI must verify syntactic, structural, and lightweight semantic assertions (links, CLI command sanity, runbook metadata).
- Publish must be an atomic operation that deposits an immutable artifact (rendered HTML + source snapshot) and a reversible pointer update.
- Owners must be explicit per runbook and enforced by branch protection rules.
- Preview environments must be stable per-PR and invalidated on new commits.

Automation specification (high level)
Goals:
- Fast feedback (CI < 10 minutes for basic checks).
- High signal (catch >95% of regressions before human review).
- Safe, auditable publish + rollback.

Required CI stages (ordered):
1) runbook-lint: YAML/markdown lints, headings, metadata present (owner, status, last_reviewed).
2) link-check: run a link validator against internal services + external URLs, with domain allowlist.
3) command-sanity: static analysis on embedded CLI snippets (simple heuristics: required flags, non-destructive defaults).
4) render-preview: build a preview site for the PR (per-PR namespace), publish to preview CDN with cache-control: no-cache.
5) smoke-tests: run short scripts that exercise any documented automation steps (e.g., sample curl to staging endpoints using service-test tokens). These use short-lived test credentials stored in Vault.
6) policy-gate: check that required approvals are present (owner, security if sensitive).
7) publish-stage: when PR is merged, create an immutable artifact and update the published pointer via an atomic transaction.

Minimum metadata schema for runbook frontmatter (YAML)
| Field | Required | Description |
|---|---:|---|
| title | yes | Human-friendly title
| owner | yes | Team alias (eng-platform/operational-runbooks) or person (github id)
| status | yes | draft | in_review | published | deprecated
| last_reviewed | yes | YYYY-MM-DD (automatically updated on publish)
| test_commands | no | short list of smoke test commands to execute in CI environment
| sensitivity | no | public | internal | restricted (requires security review)

Example: frontmatter block (YAML)
---
title: "KV prefix cache rebalancing runbook"
owner: "eng-platform/kv-cache"
status: "in_review"
last_reviewed: "2026-02-02"
test_commands:
  - "./scripts/check-cache-health --env=ci"
sensitivity: "internal"
---

Example GitHub Actions job (minimal CI snippet)
name: Runbook CI
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  lint-and-verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Setup Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v4
        with:
          python-version: '3.10'
      - name: Install tooling
        run: pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
      - name: runbook-lint
        run: runbook-lint --path runbooks/ --config .runbook-lint.yaml
      - name: link-check
        run: link-checker --root runbooks/ --allowlist domains.txt
      - name: render-preview
        run: make preview
      - name: smoke-tests
        run: ./ci/runbook-smoke-tests.sh
        env:
          VAULT_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.RUNBOOK_VAULT_TOKEN }}

Publish model (atomic)
When a PR is merged to main:
1) CI creates a release artifact: a timestamped tar.gz (rendered HTML + source snapshot + metadata.json).
2) Artifact is uploaded to the artifacts bucket with immutability flag (versioned bucket).
3) A single, atomic metadata update toggles the published pointer to the new artifact id. The metadata update is recorded in audit logs with PR author, commit sha, and release time.

Rollback procedure (operator-friendly)
1) Identify the last-good artifact id from audit log.
2) Run: redwood-docs rollback --artifact <artifact-id> --reason "<short reason>"
3) Automation verifies artifact integrity and updates published pointer.
4) CI auto-opens post-rollback PR to fix root cause if the rollback was due to a lintable failure.

Ownership, reviews, and SLAs
- Each runbook must declare a single primary owner (team or person) and a secondary owner for on-call.
- Review SLA: owners must respond to review requests within 48 hours. If no response, automatic escalation to the owning manager and an on-call reviewer pool.
- Publish SLA: after merge, automated publish must complete within 10 minutes; if publish fails, the change is not published and an alert is created (see monitoring).

Monitoring and alerting
Create the following alerts (pager/Slack routing defined in alerting matrix):
- publish-failure: alert if publish-stage fails (Severity P1 during business hours, P2 otherwise).
- smoke-test-failure: alert when smoke tests fail for merged PRs (P2).
- stale-owner-alert: runbook has status=published and last_reviewed > 365d (email weekly digest).
- rollback-detected: notify owners when automated or manual rollback occurs.

Runbook release checklist (pre-merge):
1) Frontmatter valid and owner present.
2) Lint and link-check passed.
3) Preview link is accessible and shows updated content.
4) Smoke-tests passed (if test_commands present).
5) At least one approval from owner.
6) Security approval present if sensitivity==restricted.

Operational playbook for large-scale regressions
1) If >5 publish failures in 1 hour: pause automated publishing (feature-flag disable), open incident channel, and switch to manual review queue.
2) Run a quick-hit script that scans recent merged PRs and validates artifacts; auto-rollback any artifact that fails integrity checks.
3) Triage: collect first-failure root cause and notify platform leadership.

Migration plan (pilot -> org-wide)
- Phase 1 (pilot, Q1 2026): eng-platform runbooks and 3 high-volume teams adopt the pipeline.
- Phase 2 (Q2 2026): onboard remaining ops teams; add more smoke-tests and credentialed checks.
- Phase 3 (Q3 2026): enforce metadata and owner fields with branch protections; deprecate old publish flow.

Open risks and mitigations
- Risk: Developer friction from stricter checks. Mitigation: fast local tooling (runbook-lint CLI) and clear error messages; developer preview locally.
- Risk: Secret misuse in smoke-tests. Mitigation: short-lived test credentials, tight Vault policies, and audit logs.
- Risk: Overautomation hides semantic errors. Mitigation: required periodic human review (quarterly tabletop) and sampling of published pages for quality.

Action items (next 90 days)
- [Owner: eng-platform] Implement runbook-lint v1 with improved CLI diagnostics (due 2026-03-01).
- [Owner: eng-platform] Add per-PR stable preview domains and ensure cache-control no-cache (due 2026-03-15).
- [Owner: eng-platform] Implement atomic publish artifact format and rollback CLI (due 2026-04-01).
- [Owner: eng-platform + security] Define sensitivity approval workflow and integrate into policy-gate (due 2026-04-15).

Appendix A: sample .runbook-lint.yaml (recommended)
---
rules:
  - id: frontmatter-required
    severity: error
  - id: no-broken-internal-links
    severity: error
  - id: command-sanity-check
    severity: warning
allowlist_domains:
  - internal-api.redwoodinfra.svc.cluster.local
  - status.redwood.com
---

Appendix B: diagnostics quick commands
- Local lint: runbook-lint --path runbooks/ --fix
- Preview build: make preview && open http://localhost:8000/preview/<pr-number>
- Rollback: redwood-docs rollback --artifact <artifact-id> --reason "reverted bad publish"

Related pages and references
- Runbook authoring guidelines: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/runbook-authoring-and-maintenance-guidelines-2025
- Operator onboarding curriculum: /confluence/eng-platform/team-wiki/operator-onboarding-certification-pathway-2026

Conclusion
We reduced repeat incidents by standardizing the pipeline and making publish an auditable atomic operation. The work continues: short term we must close the CI pass-rate gap and implement owner escalation. This spec is the baseline for org-wide runbook CI/CD rollout.
